# Part III: Post-Training: Adaptation, Preference, and Alignment {#part-adaptation .unnumbered}

> "Making language models bigger does not inherently make them better at
> following a user's intent."
>
> Long Ouyang et al., ["Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)

Part I produced a base model that learns the shape of text; Part II followed the
generative and multimodal architectures that branch off the same foundations.
Post-training is the stage after pre-training: where pre-training learned from
raw data, post-training adapts the resulting base model toward the behavior a
product needs. This part returns to that base model and what it still lacks.
It does not yet know which behavior a product wants from it, or which requests
a policy requires it to refuse. It has no rule for which instruction takes
precedence when instructions from two sources conflict, and given a choice
between answers, it cannot tell which a human will prefer. The weights already
contain a great deal of capability, but capability by itself is not a usable
interface. Turning it into one means directing and constraining the model,
ranking and testing its outputs, and sometimes teaching it to prefer one kind
of answer over another.

@sec-sft-peft starts with the most direct intervention: demonstrations that
reshape behavior, often through small adapters rather than a full rewrite of the
model. @sec-behavior-specs then asks what the preference signal is supposed to
mean, tracing behavior specifications, constitutions, annotator protocols, and
multi-attribute preference data before any optimizer sees them. @sec-rlhf
introduces the reward-modeling loop, in which the model learns from comparisons
between answers rather than from a single correct answer. In that loop a reward
proxy, itself a learned model, scores answers in place of a human.
@sec-dpo-variants shows why that loop can be algebraically folded into direct
preference objectives, and how the many variants differ in the constraints each
addresses and the trade-offs each makes. Learned rewards split from checkable
ones in @sec-verifiable-rewards: a checkable reward is computed by software, for
example whether generated code passes its tests. That chapter is the hinge that
connects this part to the reasoning machinery in @sec-training-to-reason.
@sec-safety-tuning follows the same post-training stack into refusals,
instruction hierarchy, and deliberation over written policy.
@sec-synthetic-data closes the circle by letting models produce, filter, judge,
and improve on data that no longer came directly from a human labeler.

As this part proceeds, the word alignment, shaping the model's behavior to be
helpful and safe rather than merely accurate, narrows. It comes to name three
decisions: which training signal to use, which of its proxy failures to accept
(cases where the model scores well on the signal without behaving as intended),
and where oversight enters the loop. Alongside compute, post-training depends
on trust in the signal that tells the model what better means.
